subject: Chemistry
sourcePolicy: Cards are derived from the uploaded NCERT Structure of Atom chapter; wording is concise active recall rather than copied textbook prose.
seeds: Atoms contain sub-atomic particles: electrons, protons and neutrons.
Cathode-ray experiments established the existence of negatively charged electrons.
Protons are positively charged nuclear particles; neutrons are electrically neutral nuclear particles.
The atom was pictured as positive matter with electrons embedded in it so the whole atom remained neutral.
Alpha-particle scattering showed that most atomic space is empty and positive charge and most mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus.
Atomic number Z equals the number of protons; mass number A equals protons plus neutrons.
Isotopes have the same atomic number but different mass numbers; isobars have the same mass number but different atomic numbers.
Electromagnetic radiation is described using wavelength and frequency; for fixed speed they are inversely related.
Energy is emitted or absorbed in discrete quanta and photon energy is E = hν.
Electrons are ejected from a suitable surface when incident radiation has sufficient frequency.
Excited atoms produce characteristic line spectra; emission and absorption spectra reveal atomic energy structure.
Hydrogen spectral lines occur in series corresponding to transitions between quantized energy levels.
Electrons occupy permitted stationary states with quantized energies; radiation accompanies transitions between allowed states.
For hydrogen-like species, allowed radius and energy depend on principal quantum number n and nuclear charge Z; energy becomes less negative as n increases.
Bohr’s model works mainly for hydrogen-like species and cannot adequately explain multi-electron atomic behaviour.
A moving material particle has wave character with wavelength λ = h/p.
Exact position and exact momentum of a microscopic particle cannot simultaneously be specified with arbitrary precision.
Electrons are described by wave functions and probability-based atomic orbitals rather than definite classical paths.
n identifies the principal shell and is related to orbital size and largely to energy.
l identifies the subshell and orbital shape; its allowed values are 0 to n−1.
m_l specifies orbital orientation and has 2l+1 allowed values for a given l.
m_s has values +1/2 or −1/2; two electrons sharing an orbital must have opposite spins.
A Bohr orbit is a proposed circular path; an orbital is a quantum-mechanical probability region. They are not synonymous.
s orbitals are spherically symmetric; p orbitals have directional lobes, with shape governed by quantum numbers.
Hydrogen orbital energy depends on n; in multi-electron atoms energy is influenced by n, l and electron interactions.
Ground-state electrons fill available orbitals in increasing order of energy, lower-energy orbitals first.
No two electrons in an atom can have the same four quantum numbers; one orbital holds at most two electrons with opposite spins.
In degenerate orbitals, pairing begins only after each orbital has first received one electron.
Electronic configuration is the distribution of electrons among atomic orbitals according to orbital energies, Aufbau, Pauli and Hund rules.
Half-filled and completely filled degenerate subshells have extra stability associated with symmetry and exchange energy.
